summary: Learners understand WHY multiplying numerator and denominator by the same whole number n (n ≥ 1) gives an equivalent fraction: splitting each of the b parts into n equal pieces makes n×b pieces in the whole and n×a shaded, so the SAME magnitude is renamed with a finer counting-unit. This is the same as multiplying by n/n, a name for 1, so the value cannot change. It extends to tenths and hundredths (3/10 = 30/100). The central contrast is with the additive error: adding a constant to top and bottom is not re-partitioning and in general changes the amount (the only exception is a fraction equal to 1, such as 2/2 → 3/3); for example, adding 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator turns 2/3 into 3/4, which is larger, not equal.
misconceptions: Additive equivalence — adding the same number to top and bottom keeps it equal (IES whole-number thinking)
Whole-number bias — (n×a)/(n×b) 'must be bigger' because the numbers are bigger (4/6 > 2/3)
Believing the value must change because 'you did something to it'

activities.title: Rename the same amount: fix the shaded length, change the labels
steps: Shade 2/3 of a bar (or mark 2/3 as a point on a number line) and keep that shaded length physically fixed — e.g. with a strip of coloured paper laid over the bar.
Subdivide every third into 2 equal pieces, then 3, then 4, and each time count the total pieces and the shaded pieces.
Record the sequence of names for the SAME shaded length: 2/3 → 4/6 → 6/9 → 8/12, and alongside each write the equation ×2, ×3, ×4 applied to both numerator and denominator.
State in your own words why the shaded amount never moved: each part was re-cut into more, smaller pieces, so both counts grew together while the whole and the shaded magnitude stayed the same.

Now test the additive move: change 2/3 by adding 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator to get 3/4. Shade 3/4 on an identical bar and lay it against the 2/3 strip. Observe that 3/4 reaches further — it is a different, larger amount.
Explain the difference out loud: multiplying re-cuts the same whole; adding a constant to each part does not re-cut anything, so here (and for any fraction not equal to 1) it lands on a new amount.
activities.insight: Multiplying numerator and denominator by a whole number n (n ≥ 1) re-partitions the same whole into finer equal parts, renaming a fixed magnitude; adding the same number to each is not re-partitioning and changes the amount (unless the fraction equals 1). Multiplying by n/n is multiplying by 1.

activities.title: Overlay check: is 4/6 bigger than 2/3?
steps: Place 2/3 and 4/6 on a shared number line (or overlay two identical strips, one cut into thirds with 2 shaded, one cut into sixths with 4 shaded).
Decide whether 4/6 lands on the same point as 2/3 or further along.
Explain why 4/6 is NOT bigger even though 4>2 and 6>3: there are more pieces, but each is smaller, so the total shaded amount is the same.
Connect this to multiplying by 2/2: state what 2/2 equals and why multiplying by it cannot change the value.
activities.insight: A larger numerator and denominator do not imply a bigger amount when both were scaled by the same factor — the pieces are correspondingly smaller, so the magnitude is unchanged.

activities.title: Generalise and bridge to tenths and hundredths
steps: Generate three fractions equivalent to 3/5 and verify each with a strip or number-line diagram.
State the general rule in words and symbols: a/b = (n×a)/(n×b) for any whole number n ≥ 1, and explain why it holds (re-partition each part into n).
Write 3/10 as hundredths: 3/10 = 30/100. State what you multiplied by (10/10) and why the value does not change.
Explain how this renaming into hundredths helps when working with decimals.
activities.insight: The equivalence rule generalises to any whole-number factor n ≥ 1 and to the tenths↔hundredths renaming that underpins decimals; the justification (re-partition = multiply by n/n = 1) is the same every time.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: Jo vs Sam
steps: Read the claim: Jo says 2/3 = 4/6 (she multiplied top and bottom by 2); Sam says 2/3 = 3/4 (he added 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator). Before drawing, PREDICT with a reason whether 2/3 and 3/4 land on the same point.
Place 2/3, 4/6 and 3/4 on one shared number line (or overlay identical strips) and observe where each falls.
Decide who is right and justify: explain why multiplying keeps the amount but adding does not.

Answer the probes: Why does multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by 2 give twice as many parts but the same amount of chocolate? When you write 2/3 as 4/6, are you multiplying by 2 or by 2/2 — and what is 2/2? Is 3/4 bigger, smaller or equal to 2/3 — prove it on a line?
activities.insight: Equivalence is renaming a fixed magnitude by re-partitioning (multiplying by a form of 1); adding 1 to each part of 2/3 lands on a different, larger amount (3/4). Stating the reason before checking exposes whether the understanding is genuine.

checkQuestion: Jo says 2/3 = 4/6 because she multiplied the top and the bottom by 2. Sam says 2/3 = 3/4 because he added 1 to the top and 1 to the bottom. Who is right? Explain, using a picture or a number line, WHY that method keeps the fraction the same and the other one doesn't.
checkAnswer: Jo is right: 2/3 = 4/6. Multiplying both by 2 splits each third into two sixths — twice as many parts, each half the size — so the shaded AMOUNT and the whole are unchanged; it is the same point renamed (and ×2/2 is multiplying by 1). Sam is wrong: adding 1 to each turns 2/3 into 3/4, a different, larger amount, because he is not re-partitioning the same whole.
